title: Linux Terminal Basics
description: Learn essential commands for directory navigation, file listing, folder creation, reading logs, and cleanup tasks.

tasks.prompt: Your Ubuntu Bash shell is in /home/user, with no symbolic links in that path. Use pwd to print the absolute path of the current working directory.
tasks.hint: Run pwd with no arguments: pwd
tasks.explanation: pwd prints the current working directory. Bash accepts -L for the logical path or -P for the physical path; they agree in this scenario because the path has no symbolic links.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, you can read and search the current directory. Use GNU ls to list all its entries, including hidden names, . and .., in long format.
tasks.hint: Combine all entries (-a) and long format (-l): ls -la
tasks.explanation: ls -a includes all directory entries, including names beginning with a dot. -l displays permissions, ownership, size, and timestamps. The flags can be combined or supplied separately.

tasks.prompt: You are in your writable /home/user directory. The name backups does not exist. Use GNU mkdir to create that subdirectory here.
tasks.hint: Give mkdir the directory name: mkdir backups
tasks.explanation: mkdir creates the named directory under the current directory. You own and can write to /home/user, so elevation is unnecessary. -p is also valid here and tolerates existing parent directories.

tasks.prompt: Your Bash shell is in /home/user. /var/log exists, has no symbolic links in its path, and is searchable by your account. Use the cd builtin to change this shell to /var/log.
tasks.hint: Use the absolute directory path: cd /var/log
tasks.explanation: cd changes the current shell working directory. The leading slash makes /var/log absolute. A shell builtin needs to run in this shell; sudo is unnecessary for a directory you can search.

tasks.prompt: You are in /var/log on an Ubuntu host with a readable regular file /var/log/syslog. Use GNU cat to print its entire contents unchanged to standard output.
tasks.hint: Supply the readable log file to cat: cat syslog
tasks.explanation: cat writes the file contents to standard output without pagination. This scenario explicitly provides syslog because not every Ubuntu installation stores logs in that file.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, temp is a disposable directory you own; you can delete all its contents and write to its parent. Use GNU rm to remove temp recursively without confirmation, even if a file is write-protected.
tasks.hint: Use recursive and force options: rm -rf temp
tasks.explanation: rm -r removes a directory and its contents; -f suppresses confirmation and ignores missing files. These options do not bypass filesystem permissions. This deletion is appropriate only because temp is explicitly disposable.
